title: Clove Oil
part: PART TWO: THE TOLL OF ONE STORY

pages.text:
*From the Bridgewater Almanac: Trolls do not need dentists. They eat their teeth.*

The clove oil hid behind the burnt sugar and dried lavender. Rue waited for the shop to empty. Her hands trembled, but only a little. She pocketed the small glass bottle. Then she scrubbed the floor.

She attacked the seams with a stiff brush and soapy water. The grime came up in grey clouds. She scrubbed until her arms ached. The tiles shone.

It was a fair trade. One small theft for one very clean shop. The hollow feeling in her chest did not go away.

Dusk arrived quickly. The sky turned a deep, bruised plum color. Rue walked to the old bridge. Same stone. Same moss. Same hump in the middle.

But this time, she did not hurry. She did not look at the water. She walked with her chin up. Her boots thudded softly on the stone. She did not feel like a girl on a dare. She felt like a friend keeping a promise.
pages.image: A small freckled girl in a mustard raincoat scrubs a stone floor with a stiff brush in a cozy tea shop, looking down with a guilty but determined expression.

pages.text:
Under the arch, Hobb sat on a flat rock with his back pressed against the stone. He looked smaller here, his mouth open like a wide, dark cave of grey-green muscle holding two small blunt tusks. His eyes were shut tight, squeezed as if he were trying to keep the pain inside.

"Right then," Rue said, setting down her bag. She climbed onto the upturned bucket she had brought, her boots gripping the wood for balance. In one hand, she held a stick; in the other, a wad of cotton. Her grip was steady because she had practiced.

"Tell me about the scones," she said. "The ones Gran makes on Tuesdays. The ones with the little bits of dried fruit."

"They are... dense," Hobb whispered. "Like bricks."

"Bricks," Rue repeated. "And the jam?"

"Sticky."

She reached into his mouth with the stick, guiding it gently past his teeth. She felt for the ache, not in a tooth but in the gum, where a pebble sat jammed deep and hard and round. She hooked the cotton around it and pulled, and it came out with a soft pop.

"There," she said. "Better?"

Hobb opened one eye. His face was slack with relief.
pages.image: A small girl stands on a wooden bucket, reaching into the wide open mouth of a large, mossy troll who sits on a rock with his eyes closed, holding a stick and cotton.

pages.text:
Hobb took the pebble and turned it over in his massive palm, where it sat as small and insignificant as a stray raisin. He looked at the stone, then at Rue, his expression shifting from pain to something much more complicated.

"I am sorry," he said, his voice dropping to a whisper. "I am so sorry. I did not mean to have a pebble in my gum, and I certainly did not mean to be in pain. I am sorry for the noise I made."

"Stop," Rue said firmly.

He stopped talking, though his ears, which looked like large, droopy leaves, still twitched.

"Stop apologizing," she continued. "It was an accident, and it is fixed. You do not have to keep saying sorry."

Hobb blinked slowly, his round spectacles mended with twine catching the dim light. "Nobody," he said quietly, "has ever told me to stop apologizing before."

He stood up, moving with the careful, deliberate caution of a large dog trying not to wake a sleeping kitten. He shuffled to the corner where a small kettle sat on a stone stove. The kettle began to hum, a low, warm vibration that sounded exactly like Biscuit purring on Gran's lap.

"It is pleased," Hobb explained, pouring the water. "It has been listening to me for a century. It knows when I am being difficult, and I have been being very difficult today."

He poured the tea into two cups. One was the size of a thimble, and the other was the size of a soup bowl.
pages.image: A large mossy troll stands in a stone arch, pouring tea from a small humming kettle into two mismatched cups while looking at a small girl with a surprised expression.

pages.text:
"Look," Hobb said, gesturing to the corner.

There were books, dozens of them, all old and soft with cracked covers, and some had water stains on the pages that looked like maps of places she had never been.

"I read everything that falls in the river," Hobb said. "Sometimes a whole chapter. Sometimes just a page. I am working on a novel about a lighthouse. It is very slow."

He pointed to a patch of moss on the wall, which was growing in a tight, small spiral.

"That is me," Hobb said. "Anxious. It grew like that this morning. When I thought you were not coming. Yesterday it was a straight line. I was feeling steady."

On a shelf sat a jar of buttons, hundreds of them in different colors and sizes, and next to it, a long stick with notches carved into it.

"The tally," Hobb said. "One notch for every story. I have been counting for three hundred years. I am getting good at it."
pages.image: A small girl looks up at a shelf of old, water-stained books and a jar of colorful buttons in a mossy stone arch, with a large troll pointing to a patch of moss growing in a spiral shape on the wall.

pages.text:
Hobb sat back down, wrapping both his hands around the warm clay of his cup, and watched the steam curl up into the dim air until it vanished.

"How did you come to be under my bridge?" he asked, his voice dropping to a low hum.

Rue looked at her own teacup, tracing the rim with a finger. "On a dare," she said. "Cedric dared me to touch the middle stone. I did it. Then I saw you crying."

Hobb went very still. He did not move for a long moment, and the only sound was the kettle humming softly in the corner, a low, contented vibration.

"Nobody," he said slowly, "has ever been dared to come and see me. It is always dared to stay away."

Rue looked at him. She saw the way his shoulders were hunched inward, the way his thick fingers were wrapped tight around the handle, holding on as if the cup were the only solid thing in the world. A sharp, sudden ache bloomed in her chest, right behind her ribs.

"I'm sorry," she said. The words tumbled out before she could catch them.

Hobb looked up. His eyes were wide, and the spectacles on his nose tilted slightly. "It isn't yours to be sorry for," he said softly.

It was the kindest thing anybody had said to her all year.
pages.image: A small girl sits on a stone step, looking at a large mossy troll who holds a teacup, their faces close together in a quiet, serious moment under a stone arch.
